title: Medieval India
summary: Muslim invaders made India their home, intermarried and adopted Indian culture; dress, speech, manners and outlook influenced each other. Society had four groups: aristocrats (the Sultan and relatives, nobility, landholders, Hindu rajas, merchants and bankers), who lived in great luxury, the Sultan outmatching all to maintain his superiority (the khutba was read and coins issued in his name on accession); priests (Brahmans and Ulema) given tax-free land; town people (merchants, traders, artisans living in their own quarters; royal karkhanas employed workers; pilgrim centres) and peasants, who paid heavy land revenue. The caste system was rigid, but ideas, food, dress and music were exchanged. Trade flourished (Banias, Marwaris, Multanis; banjaras in caravans); Delhi was the trade centre; Iltutmish introduced the silver tanka. Hinduism had degenerated into superstition and rigid caste, while Islam talked of equality, brotherhood and oneness of God; the result was the Bhakti and Sufi movements: God is supreme, all men are equal and devotion is the way to salvation.

Muslims first came as traders in the 8th century AD and became cultural ambassadors carrying Indian science to the Islamic world and Europe. Prophet Mohammad was born in AD 571 in the Quraysh tribe; his migration from Mecca to Madina in AD 622 began the Hijira era. The five principles of Islam: Tauhid (belief in Allah), Namaz (prayer five times a day), Roza (fasting in Ramzan), Zakat (alms) and Haj (pilgrimage to Mecca); his sayings are the Hadith. Sufism originated in Iran and found a congenial atmosphere in India under the Turks; Sufis believed in the unity of all religions and preached through music; their piety, tolerance, sympathy and equality attracted many Hindus of the lower classes. Pioneers: Moinuddin Chishti, Nizamuddin Auliya, Fariduddin Ganj-e-Shakar. They set up khanqahs (later centres of learning), mazars and takias, and were organised into silsilahs (Chishti, Suhrawardi, Qadiri, Naqshbandi; fourteen in the 16th century according to Abul Fazl, author of the Ain-i-Akbari) with the piri-muridi tradition; they listened to poetry and music (sama) first in Persian and later in Hindawi.

The Delhi Sultans – Mamluk Turks (1206–90), Khiljis, Tughlaqs, Sayyids and Lodis (till 1526) – ruled on behalf of the Khalifa, whose name was read with the Sultan's in the khutba. The Mughals ruled from 1526 (nominally till 1857; real rule to 1707). Sher Shah kept Humayun out for fifteen years (1540–55), built the Grand Trunk Road (Sarak-i-Azam) and struck fine coins. Akbar (1556–1605) fostered harmony, married Rajput princesses, unified the country, patronised art and learning, founded Din-i-Illahi and held debates at the Ibadat Khana in Fatehpur Sikri; his court had nine Navratnas (Birbal, Tansen, Todar Mal, Faizi, Abdur Rahim Khan-e-Khanan and others). Jahangir and Shah Jahan continued his liberal policy; Aurangzeb abandoned it and his wars led to the Mughal decline, the rise of the Marathas and Sikhs and the East India Company.

The Indo-Islamic style of architecture combined the dome, lofty minarets, arch and vault. The Mughals loved nature and built gardens: the Shalimar Bagh and Nishat Bagh in Kashmir, the three-stage Shalimar garden of Lahore, the seven-stage Pinjore garden (Chandigarh–Kalka road); the British made a three-stage garden at the Viceregal Lodge (now Rashtrapati Bhavan) and Vrindavan Gardens of Mysore followed. Pietra dura (coloured stone inlay on marble) became popular under Shah Jahan (Red Fort, Taj Mahal). Coins of Muslim kings (design, calligraphy, mint marks) are valuable sources; Muhammad Tughlaq's coins had about 25 varieties.

Bhakti saints taught like the Sufis: unite with God through love and devotion with a guru or pir; they attacked rigid religion, disregarded caste, encouraged women and taught in local languages; most came from the lower classes. In the South the Alvars and Nayanars preached bhakti. Guru Nanak (born in a Khatri family at Talwandi, now Nankana) sang hymns with the rabab, denounced idol worship, pilgrimages and rituals and demanded purity of character. Ramanuja taught in the language of common people; his disciple Ramananda (born Allahabad, educated Varanasi) carried the message north and had disciples Kabir (weaver), Sadhana (butcher), Ravidas (cobbler) and Sena (barber). Kabir (son of a Muslim weaver) called for Hindu–Muslim unity and wrote dohas; Chaitanya (Bengal, devotee of Krishna) condemned caste; Mirabai sang for Krishna; Namdev (a tailor) wrote in Marathi. In the north bhakti developed into nirguna (formless God – Nanak, Kabir) and saguna (Rama or Krishna – Tulsidas in the Ramcharitmanas, Surdas in the Sursagar, Raskhan). Features: oneness of God and brotherhood of all; surrender to God; intense personal devotion with a good moral life; the guru; the system of pahul (khande ka pahul among the Sikhs). It stimulated regional languages.
## Folk arts, painting, music and languages

Agricultural operations and festivals gave occasions for singing and dancing; every region developed its own dance with local flavour: Garba, Kalbelia, Bhangra, Giddha, Bamboo dance, Lavani. Women showed creativity in needlework: Rajasthani odhanis and tie and dye, Punjab's phulkari, Lucknow's chikan; Maharashtra's tamasha and lavani, central India's Pandavani, Merasis in the north, puppeteers, bards, mimes, acrobats, martial arts and wrestling. Painting: Humayun brought Mir Sayid Ali and Abdus Samad from Persia; Dastan-e-Amir Hamza has about 1200 paintings; Akbar employed Hindu painters (Daswant, Basawan) and Persian and Indian styles fused; Mughal painting reached its zenith under Jahangir (Ustad, Abul Hasan, Mansur); Aurangzeb withdrew patronage due to orthodox views and political preoccupations; the Rajput and Pahari schools and havelis flourished; Mughal court painters introduced landscape and signing of miniatures and artists got monthly salaries; they illustrated Changeznama, Zafarnama and Ramayana. Music: Tansen of Akbar's court composed new ragas; Hindustani school (khayal, thumri, ghazal) and Carnatic school; folk songs about Alha-Udal and Dulla Bhatti; Indo-Mughal culture: titles Badshah and Din-e-Panah, jharokha darshan, sijda. Languages: Urdu began as a camp language of Alauddin Khilji's army in the Deccan (Bijapur and Golconda cradles; Amir Khusrau); Bengali, Assamese, Oriya, Khari Boli, Punjabi, Gujarati, Marathi, Sindhi, Kashmiri, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam took present form.

Sikhism: Guru Nanak's religion; the nirguna bhakti seeds; belief in a formless God, equality, guru and pahul. Guru Arjan Dev gave the Adi Granth, the standardised Gurmukhi script and the site and foundation of the Har Mandir Sahib (Golden Temple) and Akal Takht at Amritsar; Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa in 1699 with the five Ks (kesh, kangha, kada, kirpan, kachha) and made the Adi Granth the guru. Zoroastrianism: founded by Zarathushtra in the 8th century BC in Persia; worship of fire, Ahura Mazda and Ahura Man, kindness and charity; Zend Avesta; Parsis settled at Navsari in Gujarat; Dadabhai Naoroji and Jamshedji Tata were Parsis; not a proselytising religion. South India: Cholas (9th–11th century) had a strong army and navy, Rajendra Chola conquered Indonesian islands, village democratic institutions, Kanchi a seat of learning; Vijayanagara (14th century, Hampi) and the Bahmani kingdom fought over the Raichur Doab.

vsa: Examine the religious beliefs of the Sufis.

Sufis believed in the unity of God and of all religions, the equality of all human beings, love and self-surrender to God through a pir; they preached piety, tolerance and sympathy and used poetry and music (sama) to reach ecstasy.
How did Humayun and Akbar promote the art of painting?

Humayun brought the Persian painters Mir Sayid Ali and Abdus Samad, who illustrated manuscripts like the Dastan-e-Amir Hamza; Akbar employed many Hindu painters such as Daswant and Basawan, leading to a fusion of Persian and Indian styles.
Give two reasons why Aurangzeb stopped patronising music and painting.
He held orthodox views and was preoccupied with political problems and wars.
Why were karkhanas important in medieval India?
The royal karkhanas employed artisans to produce luxury goods used by the court and also exported abroad, and they supported crafts and trade.
What did Guru Arjan Dev give to the Sikhs?
The Adi Granth (containing the sayings of five gurus and saints), the standardised Gurmukhi script, and the site and foundation of the Har Mandir Sahib (Golden Temple) and Akal Takht at Amritsar.
Name two famous Chishti Sufi saints and two folk dances of medieval India.
Moinuddin Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya; Garba and Bhangra (also Giddha, Lavani).
What was the speciality of the Hindustani school of music?
It produced sweet and rapturous melodies for different moods; ragas and raginis were personified; khayal, thumri and ghazal developed, with Tansen as pioneer.
sa: Explain the main features of the Bhakti movement.

Oneness of God and brotherhood of all human beings without discrimination of caste or gender; surrender to God, who is all-pervasive; intense personal devotion with a good moral life; the guru as spiritual guide with the pahul system; condemned rituals and sacrifices and used local languages.

sa.note: April 2022 (8 marks) asked for the development of the Bhakti movement.

sa: Describe the Mughal gardens and say why the Mughals built them.

The Mughals loved nature and built gardens with waterways, fountains and terraces, with water cascading from stage to stage with lamps behind it: Shalimar Bagh and Nishat Bagh in Kashmir, the three-stage Shalimar garden of Lahore and the seven-stage Pinjore garden near Chandigarh; the British copied them at Rashtrapati Bhavan and Vrindavan Gardens at Mysore.
Analyse the religious and social reform among the Parsis / Zoroastrianism.

Zoroastrianism was founded by Zarathushtra in the 8th century BC in Persia: worship of fire, Ahura Mazda (good) and Ahura Man (evil), kindness and charity (Zend Avesta). Parsis settled at Navsari in Gujarat; reform started among them in Mumbai in the mid-19th century; leaders include Dadabhai Naoroji and Jamshedji Tata; they set up many charities.
Write a note on Akbar's contribution to Indian culture.

Akbar fostered harmony by discouraging racial and religious bias, married Rajput princesses, unified the country with a central government, patronised art, architecture and learning, started Din-i-Illahi and held debates at the Ibadat Khana; his court had nine Navratnas such as Tansen and Todar Mal.
Describe the life of people under the Delhi Sultanate.

Society consisted of aristocrats, priests, town people and peasants; trade flourished with Delhi as centre and the silver tanka as currency; caste was rigid but Hindus and Muslims exchanged customs in food, dress and music; Islam's equality led to the Bhakti and Sufi movements.
la: Examine the development of music during the medieval period.

Under the Turko-Afghan rulers a synthesis of Indo-Iranian music began and developed further under the Mughals. Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan patronised musicians; Tansen of Akbar's court sang classical ragas and composed new ones; Shah Jahan was a good singer. Aurangzeb disliked music, yet the largest number of Persian books on classical Indian music were written in his time. The Hindustani school arose in the north with sweet melodies for moods, personified ragas and raginis, and khayal, thumri and ghazal; the Carnatic school developed in the south. Sufis used sama and Bhakti saints sang geet and qawali, and ordinary people kept folk songs about local heroes like Alha-Udal and Dulla Bhatti.
Explain the development of the Bhakti movement and its role in enriching Indian culture.

Islam's message of equality challenged the rigid caste society and gave rise to the Bhakti movement (14th–16th centuries). Saints from Alvars and Nayanars in the south, Ramanuja, Ramananda, Kabir, Nanak, Chaitanya, Mirabai, Namdev, Tulsidas and Surdas taught the oneness of God, devotion over ritual, equality and brotherhood. It split into nirguna and saguna streams. Their poetry in local languages (geet, qawali) united people and stimulated regional languages; Sikhism grew out of its nirguna branch.
Describe Mughal painting and its development from Humayun to Aurangzeb.

Humayun brought Persian painters (Mir Sayid Ali, Abdus Samad) who nurtured manuscript painting such as Dastan-e-Amir Hamza with about 1200 paintings. Akbar employed Hindu painters like Daswant and Basawan and Persian and Indian styles fused. Under Jahangir, a painter himself with Ustad, Abul Hasan and Mansur, Mughal painting reached its zenith; landscapes, portraits and miniatures developed and artists signed works and got monthly salaries. Aurangzeb withdrew patronage, but Rajput and Pahari schools flourished under princes and the rich.
Describe the rise of Sikhism and the contributions of Guru Nanak, Guru Arjan Dev and Guru Gobind Singh.

Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak, a Khatri born at Talwandi who denounced idols, pilgrimages and rituals, preached one formless God, equality and purity of conduct, and sang hymns with the rabab. The fifth guru, Arjan Dev, gave the Adi Granth, the Gurmukhi script and the Golden Temple site at Amritsar with the Akal Takht. The tenth, Gobind Singh, created the Khalsa in 1699 with the five Ks (kesh, kangha, kada, kirpan, kachha) and made the Adi Granth the guru.
